triage.name: Cervical Cancer
triage.reason: Abnormal bleeding or postcoital spotting with an abnormal Pap and cervical lesion; screening, staging, and prevention make it a core ob/gyn case.

demographics: Most common in women over age 30; median age at diagnosis is around 50
Incidence and mortality are higher in Black, Hispanic, and American Indian/Alaska Native women and in women in rural areas, largely reflecting differences in screening access
More common in countries and communities with limited access to HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screening
Rare before age 21; invasive cancer in this age group is uncommon

risk_factors.text: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), especially types 16 and 18
No or infrequent cervical cancer screening, or no follow-up after an abnormal screening result
Immunosuppression, including HIV infection, solid organ transplant, or long-term immunosuppressive therapy
Cigarette smoking or regular secondhand smoke exposure
Early age at first sexual intercourse and multiple lifetime sexual partners
Long-term use of combined oral contraceptive pills (5 or more years)
Grand multiparity (three or more full-term pregnancies)
History of other sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia

comorbidities: HIV infection or other immunocompromising condition
Prior cervical precancer (CIN 2 or CIN 3) treated or untreated
family_history: Cervical cancer or cervical precancer in a first-degree relative
social_history: Limited access to routine gynecologic care or screening
Multiple sexual partners or a partner with other partners

chief_complaints.text: I've been spotting between my periods
My discharge has changed and smells bad
I have pain down there during sex
My Pap test came back abnormal and I was sent here

hpi.onset: Gradual and often silent; bleeding or discharge may appear months after an abnormal screening result, and many women have no symptoms at diagnosis
hpi.duration: Weeks to months of intermittent symptoms before presentation
hpi.progression: Symptoms start as light postcoital or intermenstrual spotting, then become more frequent and heavier; discharge becomes watery, blood-tinged, and foul-smelling as the tumor enlarges
hpi.radiation: Pelvic or lower back discomfort may radiate to the thighs or sacrum when the tumor extends beyond the cervix
hpi.quality: Bleeding is painless and often noticed only after intercourse or douching; discharge is watery and may be blood-streaked; pain is a dull pelvic ache or sharp with intercourse
hpi.severity: Bleeding is usually light at first; pain is mild to moderate early and becomes more severe with advanced disease
hpi.timing: Bleeding most often after intercourse, between periods, or after menopause; discharge is continuous
relieving: Rest or over-the-counter acetaminophen may ease pelvic discomfort

associated_symptoms.text: Watery, blood-tinged, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge
Painful or difficult bowel movements, or rectal bleeding
Swelling of one or both legs

pertinent_negatives: Severe one-sided pelvic pain with a missed period
Heavy bleeding with clots and passage of tissue in early pregnancy
Profuse frothy or cottage-cheese discharge with intense itching
Postmenopausal bleeding while on hormone therapy
Bleeding disorder or current anticoagulant use

negatives: Prior abnormal Pap or HPV result that was never followed up
argues_against: Heavy bleeding with clots and a missed period (miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy)
Bloody diarrhea with tenesmus (colorectal or anal cancer)
Dysuria with frequency and urgency (urinary tract infection)
Fever and night sweats (pelvic inflammatory disease or lymphoma)

atypical.how_it_differs: Women over 65 may present with postmenopausal bleeding after years of normal screening, and the cancer is often more advanced because symptoms are attributed to atrophy or not evaluated.
missing_classic_features: Postcoital bleeding as the first sign

atypical.how_it_differs: Women with HIV or on immunosuppressive therapy can develop cervical cancer at a younger age, progress faster from precancer to cancer, and are more likely to have persistent HPV with multifocal disease.
missing_classic_features: Long latency from HPV exposure to cancer

atypical.how_it_differs: Bleeding in pregnancy may be attributed to pregnancy itself, delaying diagnosis; the cancer is usually found on a routine Pap or after a cervical lesion is seen at the first prenatal exam.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; may have light spotting on the pad
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, pale if bleeding has been ongoing; not toxic-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, pale, may have visible weight loss or leg swelling
general.critical: Cachectic or toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, in pain, may have brisk vaginal bleeding

labs.caveat: Anemia from chronic blood loss; a normal hemoglobin does not exclude cervical cancer.
Low ferritin supports iron deficiency from chronic tumor bleeding.
Rises with ureteral obstruction from advanced pelvic disease; also needed before contrast imaging.
Microscopic hematuria from bladder or ureteral involvement; can be confused with a urinary tract infection.
Hypercalcemia of malignancy suggests distant spread.
Low with advanced disease and poor nutritional status.
Negative. Must be checked in any woman of childbearing age with abnormal bleeding before imaging and biopsy.

imaging.preferred_when: Preferred for local staging and treatment planning

findings.text: Cervical mass with intermediate signal on T2-weighted images and enhancement after contrast
Tumor size and depth of cervical stromal invasion

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Assessment of distant spread and lymph nodes

Enlarged pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes
Liver, lung base, or peritoneal metastases

imaging.preferred_when: Initial staging when chest CT is not available

findings.text: Pulmonary nodule or mass suggesting metastasis

imaging.preferred_when: Advanced disease or when distant spread is suspected

findings.text: FDG-avid pelvic or para-aortic lymph nodes
Distant FDG-avid metastases (lung, liver, bone, supraclavicular nodes)

imaging.preferred_when: First-line evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding

findings.text: Nonspecific findings; a normal ultrasound does not exclude cervical cancer

Renal function before contrast imaging and to detect obstructive uropathy
Rules out pregnancy in any woman of childbearing age with abnormal bleeding
Pap test if not recently done; identifies abnormal squamous or glandular cells
High-risk HPV testing supports the diagnosis and risk stratification
Direct visualization and tissue sampling of the visible cervical lesion

initial.test: Pelvic MRI with and without IV contrast
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
initial.only_if: advanced disease or distant metastasis is suspected

confirmatory.why: Histologic confirmation of invasive cervical carcinoma and tumor type

supporting.why: Confirms iron deficiency from chronic blood loss

supporting.only_if: advanced or metastatic disease is suspected

supporting.why: Detects occult nodal and distant metastases
supporting.only_if: advanced disease or equivocal conventional imaging

supporting.why: Evaluates abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic mass

Replaced by CT or MRI in current practice
No role in the evaluation of abnormal vaginal bleeding or pelvic mass
Not indicated unless epigastric pain suggests pancreatitis
Not routinely needed; urinalysis is only for urinary symptoms or suspected obstruction

decision_points: Pregnancy test before imaging and biopsy in anyone who could be pregnant
Confirm the diagnosis with cervical biopsy before staging or treatment
Use MRI for local staging and CT or PET-CT for distant spread
Refer to gynecologic oncology for staging and treatment planning

criteria.name: FIGO staging of cervical cancer
criteria.summary: Stage I is confined to the cervix; stage II extends beyond the cervix but not to the pelvic wall or lower vagina; stage III involves the lower vagina, pelvic wall, hydronephrosis, or pelvic/para-aortic nodes; stage IV involves the bladder or rectal mucosa or distant organs. Staging is clinical with imaging and examination, and lymph node status is now included.
items: Stage I: confined to the cervix
Stage II: beyond the cervix, not to the pelvic wall or lower third of the vagina
Stage III: lower third of the vagina, pelvic wall, hydronephrosis, or pelvic/para-aortic nodes
Stage IV: bladder or rectal mucosa, or distant metastasis

differential.name: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (high-grade precancer)
differential.why_considered: Abnormal Pap or HPV result with postcoital spotting in a woman of screening age

history: Abnormal Pap or positive high-risk HPV test without systemic symptoms
Spotting after intercourse but no heavy or continuous bleeding
No weight loss, no leg swelling, no bowel or bladder symptoms
exam: Cervix may look normal or show a small acetowhite area on colposcopy
No friable exophytic mass, no parametrial thickening on rectovaginal exam
imaging: No cervical mass or parametrial extension on MRI

differential.name: Cervicitis (chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomonas, or herpes)
differential.why_considered: Postcoital bleeding, abnormal discharge, and dyspareunia in a sexually active woman
differential.trigger: Mucopurulent discharge, cervical motion tenderness, or fever in a sexually active patient

history: New or multiple sexual partners
Purulent or frothy discharge with odor
Fever or lower abdominal pain suggesting pelvic inflammatory disease
exam: Mucopurulent endocervical discharge
Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness
Cervix bleeds easily but has no discrete tumor
labs: Positive NAAT for chlamydia or gonorrhea
Wet mount showing trichomonads or clue cells
imaging: No cervical mass on ultrasound or MRI
Tubo-ovarian complex or fluid-filled tube if PID

differential.name: Endometrial cancer
differential.why_considered: Postmenopausal or abnormal uterine bleeding in an older woman
differential.trigger: Postmenopausal bleeding with a thickened endometrium on ultrasound

history: Postmenopausal bleeding rather than postcoital spotting
Obesity, diabetes, or unopposed estrogen exposure
No history of abnormal Pap or high-risk HPV
exam: Normal-appearing cervix
Uterus may be enlarged or tender
No cervical lesion or parametrial fixation
labs: Pap may be normal or show glandular cells of endometrial origin
imaging: Endometrial mass on MRI or biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the endometrium

differential.name: Uterine leiomyoma (fibroid) with abnormal bleeding
differential.why_considered: Heavy or irregular vaginal bleeding with pelvic pressure in a reproductive-age woman

history: Heavy menstrual bleeding with clots rather than postcoital spotting
Pelvic pressure, urinary frequency, or constipation
No abnormal Pap or high-risk HPV
exam: Enlarged, irregular, firm uterus
Normal cervix without a friable lesion
imaging: Well-circumscribed myometrial masses on ultrasound or MRI
No cervical mass or parametrial extension

history: Gradual onset of vaginal dryness and burning
Light spotting after intercourse or wiping
No foul-smelling discharge or weight loss
exam: Pale, thin, dry vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae
Cervix appears atrophic without a discrete mass
No parametrial thickening
labs: Normal Pap and negative high-risk HPV
imaging: Thin endometrium and no cervical mass on ultrasound

differential.name: Cervical polyp
differential.why_considered: Postcoital spotting with a visible cervical lesion

history: Intermittent light spotting after intercourse or douching
No systemic symptoms
exam: Smooth, soft, pedunculated lesion protruding from the external os
Does not feel friable or fixed
No parametrial thickening
imaging: No cervical mass or invasion on MRI
Polyp seen on ultrasound as a small echogenic lesion at the cervix

differential.name: Vaginal cancer
differential.why_considered: Abnormal vaginal bleeding or discharge with a vaginal lesion

history: Bleeding or discharge not clearly related to the cervix
May have prior HPV-related disease
exam: Ulcerated or exophytic lesion on the vaginal wall, not the cervix
Cervix itself appears normal
labs: Biopsy of the vaginal lesion shows carcinoma
imaging: MRI shows a vaginal mass separate from the cervix

differential.name: Metastatic disease to the cervix (e.g., from breast or colon)
differential.why_considered: Cervical mass in a woman with a known or prior malignancy

history: Known breast, colon, or other primary cancer
Symptoms may be systemic rather than vaginal bleeding
exam: Cervical mass that may be firm or nodular
Findings of the primary tumor elsewhere
labs: Tumor markers or pathology consistent with the primary cancer
imaging: Widespread metastatic disease on CT or PET-CT
Biopsy shows histology matching the primary tumor, not primary cervical carcinoma

severity.mild: Early, screen-detected or minimally symptomatic disease confined to the cervix; light postcoital spotting, no anemia, normal renal function
severity.moderate: Locally advanced disease with visible cervical tumor, persistent bleeding or discharge, mild anemia, and pelvic pain; no hydronephrosis or distant spread
severity.severe: Advanced local disease with parametrial or pelvic sidewall involvement, hydronephrosis, significant anemia, or pelvic pain requiring opioids
severity.critical: Metastatic or bulky disease with ureteral obstruction and renal failure, brisk vaginal hemorrhage, sepsis from necrotic tumor, or venous thromboembolism

red_flags.finding: Heavy vaginal bleeding with hemodynamic instability
red_flags.meaning: Tumor erosion into a vessel; needs urgent packing, embolization, or radiation

red_flags.finding: Flank pain, oliguria, or rising creatinine
red_flags.meaning: Ureteral obstruction from advanced pelvic disease; may require stenting or nephrostomy
Infected necrotic tumor or pyometra; risk of sepsis
Deep vein thrombosis or lymphatic obstruction from pelvic disease

red_flags.finding: Rectal bleeding or painful bowel movements
red_flags.meaning: Rectal or parametrial involvement suggesting stage IVA disease

red_flags.finding: Rapidly enlarging cervical mass or new supraclavicular node
red_flags.meaning: Progressive or metastatic disease requiring restaging

complications.name: Acute vaginal hemorrhage
clues: Brisk bleeding from a friable cervical tumor

complications.name: Vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistula
clues: Continuous urine or stool leakage from the vagina

complications.name: Lymphedema of the legs
clues: History of pelvic lymph node dissection or radiation

complications.name: Radiation proctitis or cystitis
clues: Rectal bleeding or hematuria after pelvic radiation

special_populations.differences: Cervical cancer is the most common gynecologic malignancy in pregnancy; abnormal bleeding may be attributed to pregnancy, delaying diagnosis. Staging is limited to avoid fetal radiation, and treatment is timed by gestational age and stage.
Women with HIV or on immunosuppressive therapy develop cervical cancer at a younger age, progress faster from precancer to cancer, and have higher rates of persistent HPV and multifocal disease.
Women over 65 may present with postmenopausal bleeding after years of normal screening; disease is often more advanced because symptoms are attributed to atrophy and screening may have stopped.
Obesity is a risk factor and can make pelvic examination and imaging more difficult, potentially delaying detection of a cervical mass.

cancer.screening: Screening for cervical cancer is recommended starting at age 21. Options include cervical cytology alone every 3 years, high-risk HPV testing alone every 5 years, or co-testing with cytology and HPV every 5 years for women aged 30 to 65. Screening may stop after age 65 in women with adequate prior normal results and no history of high-grade precancer. HPV vaccination is recommended for preteens and for everyone through age 26 who is not already vaccinated.
cancer.pathology: Most cervical cancers are squamous cell carcinomas arising from the transformation zone. Adenocarcinoma and adenosquamous carcinoma arise from glandular epithelium and are increasingly common. Rare types include small cell, neuroendocrine, and clear cell carcinoma (the latter associated with in utero DES exposure).
cancer.staging_concepts: Staging is clinical and uses pelvic examination, imaging, and sometimes examination under anesthesia. Stage I is confined to the cervix; stage II extends beyond the cervix but not to the pelvic wall or lower third of the vagina; stage III involves the lower third of the vagina, pelvic wall, hydronephrosis, or pelvic or para-aortic lymph nodes; stage IV involves the bladder or rectal mucosa or distant metastasis. Lymph node status is now included in staging.

key_questions.question: When was your last Pap test or HPV test, and what did it show?
key_questions.looking_for: No screening, overdue screening, or an abnormal result that was never followed up; supports a cervical origin

key_questions.question: Have you had any bleeding after sex or between your periods?
key_questions.looking_for: Postcoital or intermenstrual spotting, the classic early symptom of a cervical lesion

key_questions.question: Have you gone through menopause, and have you had any bleeding since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Postmenopausal bleeding; in an older woman this raises concern for cervical or endometrial cancer

key_questions.question: Has your vaginal discharge changed in color, amount, or smell?
key_questions.looking_for: Watery, blood-tinged, or foul-smelling discharge from a necrotic or enlarging tumor

key_questions.question: Do you have pelvic pain or pain during sex?
key_questions.looking_for: Dull pelvic ache or dyspareunia suggesting tumor extension beyond the cervix

key_questions.question: Any pain or difficulty with urination, blood in your urine, or trouble with bowel movements?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary or rectal symptoms suggesting bladder or rectal involvement (stage IVA)

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your legs or a dull backache?
key_questions.looking_for: Lymphedema or lumbosacral pain from pelvic sidewall or nodal disease

key_questions.question: Have you had unprotected sex, multiple partners, or a partner with other partners?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposure risk for high-risk HPV, the cause of nearly all cervical cancers

key_questions.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with HIV or another condition, or taken medicine, that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression, which speeds progression from HPV infection to cancer

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, or are you regularly around secondhand smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco exposure, a cofactor for cervical carcinogenesis

key_questions.question: Have you been vaccinated against HPV?
key_questions.looking_for: HPV vaccination status; vaccination lowers but does not eliminate risk

key_questions.question: How many full-term pregnancies have you had, and have you used birth control pills for several years?
key_questions.looking_for: Grand multiparity or long-term oral contraceptive use, both moderate risk factors

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had cervical cancer or a cervical precancer?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history that may reflect shared risk or screening patterns

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes pregnancy-related bleeding and must be known before imaging and biopsy

key_questions.question: Have you had heavy bleeding with clots, passage of tissue, or severe one-sided pelvic pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these point to miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or another acute cause rather than cancer

Watery, blood-tinged, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge and pelvic pain or dyspareunia

Parametrial thickening or fixation on rectovaginal exam suggesting extension beyond the cervix
Persistent high-risk HPV infection as the underlying cause, with smoking or immunosuppression as cofactors
Pregnancy excluded with a negative hCG before imaging and biopsy
Histologic confirmation of invasive carcinoma on cervical biopsy
Staging with pelvic MRI for local extent and CT or PET-CT for nodal and distant spread

Classic watery, foul-smelling discharge with intermenstrual bleeding
